title: Curiosity
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart closes his series on the six sense-making disciplines for teams, adapted from Richard Claydon (clarity, coherence, connection, collaboration, cooperation and curiosity), by setting out curiosity as the discipline that renews collective judgement. He argues that without curiosity a school's systems become efficient but intellectually closed, showing up as settled confidence, unexamined explanations, data read through familiar narratives and dissent treated as disruption. Leaders cannot prevent uncertainty, he says, but they can prevent premature certainty through deliberate, visible intellectual humility. He offers four practical strategies: asking what has been missed before closing a decision, surfacing the hidden assumptions a plan depends on, using the ladder of inference to separate observation from interpretation, and actively seeking perspectives from outside the immediate group. Each strategy comes with concrete in-practice moves. He concludes that curiosity does not undermine clarity or coherence but protects them from ossifying, giving teams stability with range rather than brittleness.
points: Hart's diagnosis is that the danger in leadership teams is not uncertainty but premature certainty, which curiosity exists to interrupt.
Surfacing the assumptions behind a decision shifts disagreement from personal positions to analysable reasoning about what must be true for success.
The ladder of inference is offered as a tool to slow the jump from selected data to conclusion, so narratives do not harden too early.
Leaders should treat dissent as data rather than threat and build questioning into existing decision cycles rather than occasional reflection exercises.
Curiosity is framed as the discipline that keeps the other five (clarity, coherence, connection, collaboration, cooperation) from becoming brittle.

When this question is absent, confidence hardens into assumption. Asking what has been missed does not delay action indefinitely; it strengthens it.
When assumptions remain invisible, disagreement becomes personal rather than analytical. Surfacing assumptions shifts debate from position to reasoning.

When curiosity is weak, leaders experience repeated surprises, entrenched positions and defensive reasoning. Decisions may be coherent and well coordinated, yet increasingly detached from changing reality.
They are not abstract reflective exercises to conduct occasionally; they are intellectual habits that keep systems open to learning.
Together, these six disciplines create stability with range; disciplined repetition that enables adaptability rather than brittleness.
